newsitem.title: USA: Emerging markets turmoil worries U.S., IMF - paper.
newsitem.headline: Emerging markets turmoil worries U.S., IMF - paper.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury and the International Monetary Fund are on high alert over financial turmoil in emerging markets that has sent stocks and currencies plunging lower, the Washington Post reported on Friday.
Instability in markets from Southeast Asia to Latin America and Eastern Europe is arousing concern among IMF and Clinton administration officials, who remember the 1994-95 Mexican peso crisis.

Officials worry that even if the latest turmoil does not trigger a full-blown economic slump, it could slow growth in some of the world's most vibrant economies, which have become key markets for U.S. exports, the newspaper said.
"We're certainly in close contact with the IMF, and they're certainly in close contact with the countries that are affected," one senior administration official was quoted as saying.

"We do take it seriously," Jack Boorman, director of the IMF's policy development and review department, told the paper. "We're concerned for the individual countries and we're concerned for any possibility that this starts a process of some kind, running from market to market."

Boorman said the situation differs in several ways from the Mexican crisis, since affected Southeast Asian countries "are coming off dramatically good performances" based on sound fundamentals and policies, including high savings rates, balanced budgets and effective measures to contain inflation.
The IMF has dispatched two teams to Thailand to provide advice on the troubled banking system there and the floating of the nation's currency.

The IMF's board also plans to approve a $1 billion loan for the Philippines on Friday, partly to replenish Manila's official reserves, depleted after a peso sell-off earlier this month, the Post reported.
